blocks.html: You already compare amounts with words like "three times as many" (see Times as Many). A ratio is another way to compare two amounts. It tells how much of one thing there is for every so much of another thing.
The ratio $a : b$, read "$a$ to $b$", means: for every $a$ of the first thing, there are $b$ of the second thing. The order follows the words, so the thing named first is written first.

blocks.name: tapediagram

steps: For every 3 cups of flour there are 2 cups of milk. The ratio of flour to milk is 3 : 2.
Switch the words and you switch the numbers: the ratio of milk to flour is 2 : 3.
One batch uses 3 + 2 = 5 cups in all, so the ratio of flour to the whole mix is 3 : 5.

blocks.cap: One batch of pancake batter. Press Next step to read three different ratios from the same picture.

blocks.html: Why not just say "there is 1 more cup of flour than milk"? Make a double batch: 6 cups of flour and 4 cups of milk. Now the difference is 2 cups, but the batter tastes exactly the same. What stayed the same is the mix: for every 3 cups of flour there are still 2 cups of milk. A ratio describes the mix, so it does not change when the batch grows.

blocks.text: Part to part, and part to whole

blocks.html: A bag holds 4 red marbles and 6 blue marbles. Some ratios compare one part with another part; others compare a part with the whole bag of 10.

head: Comparison
Ratio
Kind
blocks.cap: Four ratios from one bag of marbles.

blocks.html: A part-to-whole ratio is the same as a fraction of the whole: $\frac{4}{10}$ of the marbles are red. You can also write a ratio in simplest form: $4 : 6$ and $2 : 3$ describe the same mix.

blocks.title: Read the order from the words
blocks.q: A fruit bowl has 5 apples and 3 bananas. Write the ratio of bananas to apples.
steps: The words say bananas first, then apples.

blocks.title: From a ratio to a fraction
blocks.q: In a club, the ratio of girls to boys is $4 : 5$. What fraction of the club are girls?
steps: The ratio says: for every 4 girls there are 5 boys.
So each group of $4 + 5 = 9$ members has 4 girls.
Girls are 4 out of every 9 members.

blocks.html: Two slips happen a lot. One is writing the numbers in the wrong order: "cats to dogs" must start with the cats. The other is mixing up part-to-part and part-to-whole: in the club above, $\frac{4}{5}$ compares girls with boys, not with the whole club. Quick check: the fractions for all the parts must add to 1. Here $\frac{4}{9} + \frac{5}{9} = 1$, but $\frac{4}{5} + \frac{5}{4}$ is much more than 1.

Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 6.RP.A.1: understanding ratios and ratio language

blocks.html: A shade of orange paint uses 2 cans of red for every 3 cans of yellow (a ratio of $2 : 3$). To paint a bigger wall you make more batches. Two batches use 4 cans of red and 6 cans of yellow; three batches use 6 and 9.
Multiply (or divide) both numbers of a ratio by the same number to get an equivalent ratio: $2 : 3 = 4 : 6 = 6 : 9 = 8 : 12$. Equivalent ratios describe the same mix.

Multiplying both numbers by 3 is the same as making 3 batches. Each batch still has 2 cans of red for 3 cans of yellow, so the color does not change. It is the same idea as equivalent fractions: $\frac{2}{3} = \frac{4}{6}$ because both the top and the bottom were multiplied by 2.

blocks.name: ratiotable
blocks.cap: Move the marker by whole batches and add columns to the table. Then try What if we add instead? to see why adding the same amount to both does not keep the mix.

head: batches
blocks.cap: A ratio table: every column is the same mix.

blocks.title: Scale up
blocks.q: A lemonade uses 3 scoops of mix for every 4 cups of water. How many cups of water go with 15 scoops?
steps: Find the multiplier: $15 = 3 \times 5$, so this is 5 batches.
Multiply the water by the same 5: $4 \times 5 = 20$.
Check: $3 : 4$ and $15 : 20$ are equivalent, since both numbers were multiplied by 5.

blocks.title: Scale down, then up
blocks.q: A paint uses 6 cans of red for every 9 cans of yellow. How many cans of yellow go with 10 cans of red?
steps: 10 is not a whole-number multiple of 6, so first make the ratio smaller.
Now $10 = 2 \times 5$, so multiply both parts of $2 : 3$ by 5: $10 : 15$.

blocks.html: Adding the same amount to both numbers does not make an equivalent ratio. $2 : 3$ and $4 : 5$ look alike, but in $2 : 3$ the red is $\frac{2}{3}$ of the yellow, and in $4 : 5$ it is $\frac{4}{5}$ of the yellow, a redder orange. Quick check: an equivalent ratio has one multiplier that works for both numbers. $2 \times 2 = 4$, but $3 \times 2 = 6$, not 5.

sources.name: OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e, section 5.6 Ratios and Rate
Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 6.RP.A.3a: tables of equivalent ratios

blocks.html: A ratio table is a list of pairs, and you already know how to plot pairs as points (see Graphing Points in a Problem). A recipe uses 1 cup of rice for every 3 cups of water. Its equivalent ratios are the pairs $(1, 3)$, $(2, 6)$, $(3, 9)$ and $(4, 12)$.

blocks.name: g6-plane
blocks.cap: Cups of rice across, cups of water up. Every pair from the ratio table sits on one straight line through (0, 0).

blocks.html: When you graph equivalent ratios, the points lie on a straight line through $(0, 0)$. Each step of 1 to the right climbs the same amount: the unit rate.

Why through $(0, 0)$? Zero batches use 0 cups of rice and 0 cups of water. Why a straight line? Every extra cup of rice brings exactly 3 more cups of water, so every step to the right climbs by the same 3. A path that always climbs the same amount for the same step is a straight line.

blocks.title: Use the line
blocks.q: The graph of a ratio goes through $(0, 0)$ and $(4, 10)$. What is $y$ when $x = 6$?
steps: Divide both by 2: $(2, 5)$ is on the line too.

blocks.title: Find the point at $x = 1$
blocks.q: The point $(5, 8)$ is on the graph of a ratio. Which point on the line has $x = 1$?
steps: The y-value at $x = 1$ is the unit rate: 1.6 for each 1.

blocks.html: Points that line up are not always a ratio. The pairs $(1, 4)$, $(2, 5)$, $(3, 6)$ also make a straight line, but each $y$ is $x + 3$: adding the same amount, not scaling. Their line crosses the y-axis at 3, not at 0. Quick check: divide $y$ by $x$ for every pair. A ratio gives the same answer each time ($\frac{3}{1} = \frac{6}{2} = \frac{9}{3}$); these give $4$, $2.5$ and $2$.

blocks.name: g6-plane
blocks.cap: Adding 3 each time: the points line up, but the line starts at (0, 3), so these pairs are not equivalent ratios.

Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 6.RP.A.3a: plotting pairs from ratio tables

blocks.html: A rate is a ratio that compares two different kinds of things, like miles and hours. A unit rate tells how much for one: miles for one hour, dollars for one pound. Unit rates are equivalent ratios whose second number is 1.

blocks.name: tapediagram

steps: A car goes 120 miles in 3 hours at a steady speed.
Split the 120 miles into 3 equal parts, one for each hour.
Each part is 120 ÷ 3 = 40 miles: 40 miles per hour.

blocks.cap: Splitting the miles into one equal piece for each hour.

blocks.html: To find a unit rate, divide. The quantity you are counting goes on top, and the "per" thing goes underneath: $\frac{120 \text{ miles}}{3 \text{ hours}} = 40$ miles per hour.

To get from 3 hours down to 1 hour, divide by 3. To keep the ratio the same, divide the miles by 3 as well: $120 : 3 = 40 : 1$. Writing it as a fraction says the same thing, because a fraction is a division: $\frac{120}{3} = 120 \div 3 = 40$.

blocks.title: A price per item
blocks.q: 4 notebooks cost \$7. What is the price of one notebook?
steps: Price per notebook means dollars for 1 notebook: dollars ÷ notebooks.

blocks.title: Two unit rates from one ratio
blocks.q: A printer prints 90 pages in 6 minutes. Find pages per minute and minutes per page.
steps: Minutes per page: $6 \div 90 = \frac{1}{15}$ of a minute (4 seconds).
blocks.a: 15 pages per minute, or $\frac{1}{15}$ minute per page.

blocks.html: Dividing in the wrong order gives the other unit rate. For 120 miles in 3 hours, $3 \div 120 = \frac{1}{40}$ is hours per mile, not miles per hour. Quick check: say the units out loud. The word after "per" is the one you divide by. Then ask if the size makes sense: a car covers many miles in an hour, so miles per hour should be a big number.

sources.name: OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e, section 5.6 Ratios and Rate
Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 6.RP.A.2: unit rates

blocks.html: Once you know a unit rate, many problems become one multiplication or one division. Unit rates also make fair comparisons: when both offers are written "per one", you are comparing like with like.
Find the rate for one unit. Then: total = rate $\times$ number of units, and number of units = total $\div$ rate.

A unit rate is the cost, distance or amount for exactly one unit. Seven notebooks cost 7 times the price of one. A trip at 50 miles per hour takes one hour for every 50 miles, so the number of hours is how many 50s fit in the distance.

blocks.title: The better buy
blocks.q: Cereal comes in a 12-ounce box for \$3.00 or a 20-ounce box for \$4.40. Which is the better buy?
steps: 22 cents is less than 25 cents per ounce.
blocks.a: The 20-ounce box is the better buy.

blocks.name: ratiotable

task.text: A car goes 110 miles in 2 hours. How far does it go in 5 hours? Move the marker to 5 hours.

blocks.cap: Hours on the top line, miles below. Find the miles for 1 hour first, then for 5 hours.

blocks.title: Constant speed
blocks.q: A cyclist rides 36 miles in 3 hours at a steady speed. How long does it take to ride 60 miles?
steps: Each hour covers 12 miles, so count the 12s in 60: $60 \div 12 = 5$.

blocks.title: How many can you buy?
blocks.q: 6 bagels cost \$4.50. How many bagels can you buy with \$12?

blocks.html: Comparing the totals instead of the unit prices. The 20-ounce box costs more in total (\$4.40 against \$3.00), so it can look like the worse deal, but you also get more cereal. Quick check: before comparing, make sure both numbers are "per one" of the same unit.

blocks.html: Percent means "per hundred" (just as there are 100 cents in a dollar). A percent is a ratio whose second number is 100, so you can read it in hundredths, the place you met in decimals.

blocks.name: decimalgrid
blocks.cap: A hundred grid: each small square is 1%, so 35 squares are 35%. Tap or drag to shade other amounts.

blocks.html: Because the whole is cut into 100 equal parts, a percent counts hundredths. That is why 35% is the same number as $\frac{35}{100}$ and as 0.35 (35 hundredths). To write a part out of some other whole as a percent, make an equivalent ratio with 100 as the whole.

blocks.title: Out of 20
blocks.q: 7 of the 20 questions on a quiz were about fractions. What percent is that?

blocks.title: A tiny percent
blocks.q: Write $0.5\%$ as a decimal.
steps: Dividing by 100 moves each digit two places to the right: $0.005$.
That is half of one hundredth.

head: Percent
Fraction
Decimal
blocks.cap: Three names for each amount.

blocks.html: $0.5\%$ is not $50\%$. Fifty percent is half of the whole; half a percent is half of one hundredth, which is 1 part in 200. Quick check: write both as decimals. $50\% = 0.50$ but $0.5\% = 0.005$, a hundred times smaller. On the grid, 50% fills half the squares; 0.5% would fill half of a single square.

blocks.name: decimalgrid
blocks.cap: Left: 50% is half the grid. Right: 1% is one small square, and 0.5% is only half of that one square.

sources.name: OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e, section 6.1 Understand Percent
Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 6.RP.A.3c: percent as a rate per 100

blocks.html: A percent tells what part of a whole you want, out of 100 (see Percent Means per 100). To find 30% of 80, think of 80 split into 100 equal tiny parts and take 30 of them.
To find a percent of a number, find 10% (or 1%) of it first, then build up. Or multiply: $p\%$ of $n$ is $\frac{p}{100} \times n$.

blocks.name: percentbar
blocks.cap: The amount 80 on top is 100% below. Move the marker to 30% and read the amount above it.

blocks.html: Taking 30 of the 100 tiny parts of 80 is $\frac{30}{100} \times 80$. Splitting into 10 equal parts first is a friendlier path to the same place: 10% of 80 is $80 \div 10 = 8$, and 30% is three of those tenths, $3 \times 8 = 24$. Both ways give 24, because $\frac{30}{100} = 3 \times \frac{1}{10}$.

blocks.title: Build from 10%
blocks.q: Find 30% of 80.

blocks.title: A tip
blocks.q: A family leaves a 15% tip on a \$40 meal. How much is the tip?

blocks.title: Use a fraction
blocks.q: What is 75% of 36?

blocks.html: Dividing by the percent: "30% of 80" is not $80 \div 30$. Quick check with size: 30% is less than half, so the answer must be less than half of 80, which is 40. And 100% of a number is the number itself, so 120% of 80 must be more than 80.

sources.name: OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e, section 6.2 Solve General Applications of Percent
Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 6.RP.A.3c: finding a percent of a quantity

blocks.html: Sometimes you know a part and its percent, but not the whole. "12 is 40% of what number?" You can still use what you know about percents of a number: work backward to 100%.
If a part is $p\%$ of the whole, use the part to find 10% (or 1%, or another easy percent), then multiply up to 100%.

blocks.name: percentbar
blocks.cap: The part, 12, sits at 40%. The whole bar is 100%, and it is unknown. Press Next step to find 10% and then 100%.

blocks.html: The part and the whole are in the same ratio as the percent and 100: $12 : \text{whole} = 40 : 100$. Equivalent ratios do the rest: divide by 4 to get "3 is 10%", then multiply by 10 to get "30 is 100%".

head: amount
blocks.cap: A ratio table from the part to the whole: ÷ 4, then × 10.

blocks.title: Work back to 100%
blocks.q: 12 is 40% of what number?

blocks.title: Saving for a bike
blocks.q: Ana has saved \$45. That is 60% of the price of a bike. What is the price?

blocks.html: Multiplying the part by the percent. $12 \times 40\% = 4.8$ answers a different question: "What is 40% of 12?" Here 12 is the part, not the whole. Quick check: when the percent is less than 100%, the whole must be bigger than the part. 4.8 is smaller than 12, so it cannot be the whole.

Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 6.RP.A.3c: finding the whole from a part and the percent

blocks.html: Every pair of units makes a ratio: 1 foot : 12 inches, 1 hour : 60 minutes, 1 kilogram : 1,000 grams. In Grade 5 you converted with these facts. Now treat each one as a rate and scale it like any ratio.
Use the ratio between the units. Going to a smaller unit, multiply (you need more of them). Going to a larger unit, divide (you need fewer).

blocks.name: ratiotable

task.text: Move the marker to 42 inches. How many feet is that?

blocks.cap: Feet on the top line, inches below. The marker moves in half feet.

blocks.html: Since 1 foot : 12 inches is a ratio, it scales: 3 feet : 36 inches, 4.5 feet : 54 inches. Another way to see it: the fraction $\frac{12 \text{ inches}}{1 \text{ foot}}$ is equal to 1, because its top and bottom are the same length. Multiplying by 1 never changes an amount; it only changes the units we use to name it.

blocks.title: To a larger unit
blocks.q: Convert 54 inches to feet.
steps: Feet are bigger than inches, so there will be fewer of them: divide.

blocks.title: To a smaller unit
blocks.q: Convert 2.5 hours to minutes.
steps: Minutes are smaller, so there will be more of them: multiply.

blocks.title: Multiply by a fraction worth 1
blocks.q: How many inches are in 3 yards?

blocks.html: Multiplying when you should divide. Changing 54 inches to feet by multiplying gives 648 "feet", longer than a city block. Quick check before you compute: which unit is bigger? A bigger unit needs a smaller number, so feet must come out less than the number of inches.

Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 6.RP.A.3d: converting measurement units with ratios

blocks.html: Division asks two kinds of question. $12 \div 3$ can mean "how many 3s fit in 12?" or "share 12 into 3 equal groups." In Grade 5 you used both meanings with whole numbers and unit fractions. The "how many fit?" meaning works for any fractions.
$\frac{3}{4} \div \frac{1}{8}$ asks: how many $\frac{1}{8}$s fit in $\frac{3}{4}$? Write both with the same denominator and count pieces: $\frac{6}{8} \div \frac{1}{8} = 6$.

blocks.name: tapediagram

steps: Three fourths of the bar is shaded.
Cut the whole bar into eighths. The shaded part is the same as 6 eighths.
So six pieces of size 1/8 fit in 3/4: 3/4 ÷ 1/8 = 6.

blocks.cap: Counting eighths inside three fourths. Press Next step.

blocks.html: Once both numbers are counted in eighths, the question is about pieces of one size: 6 eighths ÷ 1 eighth works like 6 apples ÷ 1 apple. The size of the pieces does not matter any more, just as $600 \div 100 = 6 \div 1$ when you count in hundreds.

blocks.title: Whole groups
blocks.q: How many $\frac{2}{3}$-cup scoops are in 2 cups of rice? Find $2 \div \frac{2}{3}$.
steps: Each scoop is 2 thirds. How many groups of 2 thirds are in 6 thirds? $6 \div 2 = 3$.

blocks.title: Part of a group
blocks.q: Find $\frac{5}{6} \div \frac{1}{3}$.
steps: Use sixths for both: $\frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{6}$, so the question is $\frac{5}{6} \div \frac{2}{6}$.
How many groups of 2 sixths fit in 5 sixths? Two full groups use 4 sixths, and 1 sixth is left.
The leftover is 1 of the 2 sixths a group needs: half a group.
So $2$ groups and $\frac{1}{2}$ of a group.

blocks.html: Expecting the answer to be small. When you divide by a fraction less than 1, many small pieces fit, so the quotient is bigger than the number you started with: $\frac{3}{4} \div \frac{1}{8} = 6$. Quick check: if you divide by a number less than 1 and get a smaller answer, something went wrong.

The sharing meaning works too: "if $\frac{3}{4}$ cup is $\frac{1}{8}$ of a batch, how much is a whole batch?" Eight eighths make the batch, so it is $8 \times \frac{3}{4} = 6$ cups. Same answer, as it must be.

sources.name: OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e, section 4.2 Multiply and Divide Fractions
Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 6.NS.A.1: interpreting division of fractions

blocks.html: You have seen that $\frac{3}{4} \div \frac{1}{8}$ asks how many eighths fit in three fourths (see What Dividing by a Fraction Means). Renaming with a common denominator always works, and it leads to a quick rule.
To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal: $\frac{a}{b} \div \frac{c}{d} = \frac{a}{b} \times \frac{d}{c}$. Keep the first fraction and flip only the divisor.

blocks.name: tapediagram

steps: Cut both bars into twelfths: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12.
How many groups of 9 twelfths fit in 8 twelfths? Not even one whole group.
The 8 pieces are 8 of the 9 pieces a group needs, so 2/3 ÷ 3/4 = 8/9.

blocks.cap: Two thirds against three fourths, both cut into twelfths.

blocks.html: With a common denominator, $\frac{2}{3} \div \frac{3}{4} = \frac{8}{12} \div \frac{9}{12}$, which counts groups of 9 pieces in 8 pieces: $\frac{8}{9}$. The rule gives the same: $\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{4}{3} = \frac{8}{9}$. This always happens: $\frac{a}{b} \div \frac{c}{d} = \frac{ad}{bd} \div \frac{bc}{bd} = \frac{ad}{bc}$, which is exactly $\frac{a}{b} \times \frac{d}{c}$. Another way to see it: dividing by $\frac{c}{d}$ undoes multiplying by $\frac{c}{d}$, and so does multiplying by $\frac{d}{c}$, because $\frac{c}{d} \times \frac{d}{c} = 1$.

blocks.title: Two fractions
blocks.q: Find $\frac{3}{4} \div \frac{2}{5}$.

blocks.title: A mixed number
blocks.q: Find $2\frac{1}{2} \div \frac{3}{4}$.
steps: Write the mixed number as a fraction: $2\frac{1}{2} = \frac{5}{2}$.
As a mixed number, $3\frac{1}{3}$. That makes sense: about three $\frac{3}{4}$s fit in $2\frac{1}{2}$.

blocks.title: A whole number
blocks.q: Find $6 \div \frac{3}{5}$.

blocks.html: Flipping the wrong fraction, or both. $\frac{3}{4} \div \frac{2}{5}$ is not $\frac{4}{3} \times \frac{5}{2}$: only the divisor, the number you divide by, is flipped. Quick check: multiply your answer by the divisor. You should get the first number back.

blocks.html: Now that you can divide fractions, the harder part of a story problem is noticing that it is division. Look for one of two questions: "how many of these fit in that?" or "how much is one whole group?"
Divide when you know a total and either the size of one group (to find how many groups) or how many groups there are, even part of a group (to find the size of one group).

Every division undoes a multiplication: $\text{groups} \times \text{size of a group} = \text{total}$. If you know the total and one of the other two, division finds the missing one. That is true for $3 \times 4 = 12$, and it is just as true when the numbers are fractions.

blocks.title: How many pieces?
blocks.q: A ribbon is $2\frac{1}{4}$ yards long. It is cut into pieces $\frac{3}{8}$ yard long. How many pieces are there?
steps: How many $\frac{3}{8}$s fit in $2\frac{1}{4}$? That is $2\frac{1}{4} \div \frac{3}{8}$.

blocks.title: How much is one whole?
blocks.q: $\frac{3}{4}$ cup of water fills $\frac{1}{2}$ of a bottle. How much water fills the whole bottle?
steps: The total for half a bottle is known. One whole bottle is one group, so divide: $\frac{3}{4} \div \frac{1}{2}$.
Makes sense: two halves of $\frac{3}{4}$ cup each make $1\frac{1}{2}$ cups.

blocks.name: tapediagram

steps: Half of the bottle holds 3/4 cup.
The other half holds the same amount.

blocks.cap: The bottle in two halves. Each half holds the same amount.

blocks.title: A missing side
blocks.q: A rectangle has an area of $\frac{3}{5}$ square meter. Its length is $\frac{3}{4}$ meter. How wide is it?
steps: Area = length × width, so width = area ÷ length.

blocks.html: Dividing in the wrong order. In the bottle story, $\frac{1}{2} \div \frac{3}{4} = \frac{2}{3}$ would mean the whole bottle holds less than its half. Quick check: say what each number means, then ask if the answer is sensible. The whole bottle must hold more than the $\frac{3}{4}$ cup in half of it.

blocks.html: You have divided by two-digit numbers already. Fluency means doing it reliably: estimate each digit, keep the places lined up, and check by multiplying.
Work from the left. At each place: divide (how many times does the divisor fit?), multiply, subtract, bring down the next digit. Write a 0 in the quotient when the divisor does not fit.

Long division is a fast way of taking away big equal groups. For $8,736 \div 24$: 300 groups of 24 use 7,200, leaving 1,536; 60 more groups use 1,440, leaving 96; 4 more groups use 96. That is $300 + 60 + 4 = 364$ groups. The algorithm does exactly these steps, writing each count in its own place.

blocks.name: areamodel
blocks.cap: Division as a missing side: a rectangle 24 wide with area 8,736 is 300 + 60 + 4 = 364 long.

blocks.title: Four digits by two digits
steps: 24 does not fit in 8, so start with 87. $87 \div 24$: 3 times. $3 \times 24 = 72$; $87 - 72 = 15$.
Bring down the 6: 96. $96 \div 24 = 4$. $4 \times 24 = 96$; nothing is left.

blocks.title: A zero in the quotient
steps: Bring down the 7: 24 does not fit in 7, so write 0 in the quotient.

blocks.html: Skipping the 0 when the divisor does not fit. Without it, $4,872 \div 24$ comes out as 23. Quick check: estimate first. $4,800 \div 24 = 200$, so an answer near 23 is far too small.

blocks.html: In Grade 5 you added, subtracted, multiplied and divided by decimals. Here are the four rules side by side, with the reason each one works.

Add or subtract: line up the decimal points. Multiply: multiply as whole numbers, then give the product as many decimal places as the factors have together. Divide: move the decimal point in both numbers until the divisor is a whole number.

Each rule keeps place value honest. Lining up the points adds tenths to tenths and hundredths to hundredths. In $2.4 \times 1.5$, you are multiplying 24 tenths by 15 tenths, and tenths times tenths are hundredths: 360 hundredths, or 3.60. In a division, multiplying both numbers by 10 does not change the quotient, just as $6 \div 3 = 60 \div 30$.

blocks.name: areamodel
blocks.cap: $2.4 \times 1.5$ as an area: $2 \times 1 + 2 \times 0.5 + 0.4 \times 1 + 0.4 \times 0.5 = 3.6$.

blocks.title: Add with different places
steps: Line up the points and write $12.5$ as $12.500$.

blocks.title: Multiply
blocks.q: Find $2.4 \times 1.5$.
steps: The factors have $1 + 1 = 2$ decimal places, so the product has 2: $3.60$.

blocks.title: Divide by a decimal
steps: Multiply both by 10 so the divisor is whole: $75.6 \div 4$.

blocks.html: Lining up the last digits instead of the decimal points. Written that way, $12.5 + 3.875$ adds 5 tenths to 5 thousandths. Quick check: round first. $12.5 + 3.875$ is about $13 + 4 = 17$, so an answer like 4.0 or 160 cannot be right.

blocks.html: You know how to find multiples and how to write a prime factorization. Two numbers often share factors and share multiples, and two of those shared numbers are special.

The greatest common factor (GCF) is the biggest number that divides both numbers. The least common multiple (LCM) is the smallest number that both numbers divide into. For 12 and 18: GCF = 6, LCM = 36.

Prime factors show why. $12 = 2 \times 2 \times 3$ and $18 = 2 \times 3 \times 3$. A common factor can only use primes that both numbers have, and the most they share is one 2 and one 3: GCF $= 2 \times 3 = 6$. A common multiple must contain each number's whole factorization, so it needs two 2s and two 3s: LCM $= 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 3 = 36$.

steps: The biggest number on both lists is 12.

steps: Stop at the first one that 6 also divides: 8 no, 16 no, 24 yes.

blocks.title: Which one does the story need?
blocks.q: Hot dogs come in packs of 10 and buns in packs of 8. What is the smallest number of each you can buy to have the same number of hot dogs and buns?
steps: Buying packs adds up 10 at a time and 8 at a time, so we want a number that is a multiple of both.
Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30, 40. 40 is also a multiple of 8.
That is 4 packs of hot dogs and 5 packs of buns.

blocks.html: Using the wrong one. Splitting things into identical groups with nothing left over needs a number that divides both amounts: a factor, the GCF. Things that repeat until they line up again need a multiple: the LCM. Quick check: the GCF can never be bigger than the smaller number, and the LCM can never be smaller than the bigger number.

blocks.html: Once you can find the greatest common factor of two numbers, you can write their sum as one product. This is the distributive property used backward, and it is the same move you will soon make with letters.
To factor a sum, pull out the GCF and divide each number by it: $36 + 8 = 4(9 + 2)$, because $36 = 4 \times 9$ and $8 = 4 \times 2$.

Its area is $4(9 + 2) = 44$, which is $36 + 8$. That is the distributive property: $4(9 + 2) = 4 \times 9 + 4 \times 2$.

blocks.html: On the coordinate plane you have used numbers that start at 0 and grow. But many things go in two directions from a starting point: warmer or colder than zero degrees, above or below sea level, money in or money out.

Choose a zero point. Numbers on one side of it are positive, numbers on the other side are negative, written with a minus sign: 8 degrees below zero is $-8$. Zero itself is neither positive nor negative.

blocks.name: numberline
blocks.cap: A number line works like a thermometer turned on its side: colder to the left of 0, warmer to the right.

blocks.html: A measurement like "8 degrees" is not complete until you know which way from zero it goes. The sign carries the direction and the digits carry the size. That lets one number line hold both directions, with 0 as the starting point in the middle.

blocks.html: Every positive number has a partner on the other side of 0. Those partners are called opposites.
Opposites are the same distance from 0, on opposite sides: 3 and $-3$. The minus sign can be read "the opposite of", so $-(-3)$ is the opposite of $-3$, which is $3$.

blocks.name: g6-line
blocks.cap: 3 and −3 are each 3 units from 0.

blocks.html: Taking the opposite flips a number across 0 to the same distance on the other side. Flip 3 and you land on $-3$. Flip $-3$ and you land back on 3. So $-(-3) = 3$: two flips bring you home. The number 0 does not move when you flip it, so 0 is its own opposite.

blocks.q: What is the opposite of $7.5$?
steps: Its opposite is 7.5 units left of 0.

blocks.title: Opposite of an opposite
blocks.q: Simplify $-(-12)$.
steps: The opposite of $-12$ flips back across 0.

blocks.title: Three flips
blocks.q: Simplify $-(-(-2))$.
steps: Then $-(2) = -2$. Three flips end on the negative side.

blocks.html: Thinking that two minus signs "stay negative", so $-(-3) = -3$. Quick check with the picture: each minus sign is one flip across 0. An even number of flips ends where you started.

blocks.html: You can place opposites of whole numbers. Fractions and decimals have opposites too, and they fill in the spaces between the negative integers.
To place a negative fraction or decimal, find its opposite on the positive side, then reflect across 0. $-2.5$ is halfway between $-3$ and $-2$, because $2.5$ is halfway between 2 and 3.

blocks.name: g6-line
blocks.cap: Mirror images: 2.5 and −2.5 are the same distance from 0.

blocks.html: $-2.5$ means "2.5 units to the left of 0". Walking left from 0, you pass $-1$, then $-2$, and then you still have half a unit to go. So $-2.5$ is past $-2$, halfway to $-3$. Going left, the numbers get smaller, so the farther left a number is, the more negative it is.

blocks.name: numberline
blocks.cap: Your turn on a line marked in halves.

blocks.title: A negative fraction
blocks.q: Where is $-\frac{3}{4}$?
steps: $\frac{3}{4}$ is between 0 and 1, three quarters of the way to 1.
Reflect: $-\frac{3}{4}$ is between $-1$ and 0, three quarter-steps left of 0.

blocks.title: Read a point
blocks.q: A number line from $-2$ to 0 is cut into fourths. Point P is 3 small steps left of $-1$. What number is P?
steps: Three quarter-steps left of $-1$ means $\frac{3}{4}$ farther from 0 than $-1$: that is $-1\frac{3}{4}$.

blocks.html: Putting $-2.5$ between $-2$ and $-1$, as if you read the negative side from left to right like the positive side. Quick check: $-2.5$ is farther from 0 than $-2$ is (2.5 units against 2), so it must sit to the left of $-2$.

blocks.html: Once numbers are on a number line, ordering them is a matter of looking left and right.
Numbers increase from left to right. Farther left is less: $-8 < -3$, even though 8 is greater than 3.

blocks.name: numberline
blocks.cap: −8 is farther left than −3, so −8 < −3.

blocks.html: Think of temperatures. $-8$ degrees is 8 degrees below zero and $-3$ degrees is 3 below zero, so $-8$ is colder: it is less. For negative numbers, a bigger distance from 0 means a smaller number, because you have gone farther in the "less" direction.

blocks.title: Compare two negatives
blocks.q: Which is greater, $-1.5$ or $-1.25$?
steps: $-1.5$ is 1.5 units left of 0; $-1.25$ is 1.25 units left of 0.
$-1.25$ is closer to 0, so it is farther right.

blocks.title: Order a list
blocks.q: Write $-1.5$, 2, $-\frac{3}{4}$ and $-2$ from least to greatest.
steps: The negatives come first. Of $-2$, $-1.5$ and $-\frac{3}{4}$, the one farthest from 0 is the least: $-2$.

blocks.title: In a story
blocks.q: At dawn it was $-12$ °F in Fargo and $-7$ °F in Duluth. Write an inequality and say which city was colder.

blocks.html: Saying $-8 > -3$ because $8 > 3$. That compares the distances from 0, not the numbers. Quick check: picture a thermometer. Which reading is lower? The lower one is the lesser number.

blocks.html: You can order numbers by their position on the line. Sometimes we care instead about how far a number is from 0, not which side it is on. You saw this with opposites: 3 and $-3$ are the same distance from 0.
The absolute value of a number is its distance from 0, written $|a|$. Distance is never negative: $|-5| = 5$ and $|5| = 5$.

blocks.name: g6-line
blocks.cap: Both numbers are 5 units from 0.

blocks.html: Absolute value counts steps from 0, and you cannot walk a negative number of steps. So it keeps the size of a number and forgets its direction. That is why it is useful for things like the size of a debt or how far below sea level a submarine is.

blocks.title: Which numbers?
blocks.q: Find every number $x$ with $|x| = 6$.
steps: We need every number 6 units from 0.
One is 6 units right of 0 and one is 6 units left.

blocks.title: Bigger debt, smaller balance
blocks.q: Jo’s balance is $-30$ dollars and Ana’s is $-10$ dollars. Who owes more?
steps: A negative balance is a debt. The size of the debt is the absolute value: $|-30| = 30$ and $|-10| = 10$.

head: Balance
Compared as numbers

blocks.cap: Order and size answer different questions.

blocks.html: Mixing up order and size. "$-30$ is less than $-10$, so it is less debt" sounds right but is backward: $-30$ is less as a number (farther left), yet its size, the debt, is bigger. Quick check: ask whether the question is about position ("which is less?") or size ("how much is owed?"). Size questions need absolute value.

blocks.html: In Grade 5 you plotted points to the right of and above the origin (see Points on the Coordinate Plane). Now each axis is a full number line, with negative numbers too, so the plane has four parts.

A point $(x, y)$: start at the origin, move $x$ left or right, then $y$ down or up. The four quadrants are numbered counterclockwise from the top right: I $(+, +)$, II $(-, +)$, III $(-, -)$, IV $(+, -)$.

blocks.name: g6-plane
blocks.cap: One point in each quadrant. B is A reflected across the y-axis; D is A reflected across the x-axis.

blocks.html: The x-axis is a number line, so negative x means left. The y-axis is a number line standing up, so negative y means down. Reflecting a point across an axis puts it the same distance from that axis on the other side, so one coordinate changes to its opposite: across the x-axis $(x, y) \to (x, -y)$, across the y-axis $(x, y) \to (-x, y)$.

blocks.name: geoboard
blocks.cap: Drag P around the plane and watch its coordinates change sign from quadrant to quadrant.

blocks.title: Plot and name the quadrant
blocks.q: Plot $(-3, 2)$. Which quadrant is it in?
steps: Start at the origin. $x = -3$: move 3 left.
Left and up is Quadrant II.

blocks.title: Reflect
blocks.q: Reflect $(4, -1)$ across the y-axis.
steps: Across the y-axis the point moves left or right, so x changes sign.

blocks.title: On an axis
blocks.q: Where is $(0, 4)$?
steps: $y = 4$: 4 up. The point is on the vertical axis.
blocks.a: On the y-axis (not in any quadrant).

blocks.html: Two mix-ups are common. One is swapping the coordinates and plotting $(-3, 2)$ at $(2, -3)$: x always comes first, like "walk before you climb". The other is putting $(0, 4)$ on the x-axis. Quick check: a 0 in the x spot means you never moved sideways, so you are still on the y-axis.

blocks.html: When two points share a coordinate, the segment between them is horizontal or vertical, and its length comes straight from the other coordinates. You will use absolute value to handle points in different quadrants.
If two points have the same y (or the same x), the distance is the gap between the other coordinates. On the same side of 0, subtract their absolute values; on opposite sides, add them.

blocks.cap: A(−3, 2) and B(4, 2) share y = 2. Drag the points and watch the length.

blocks.html: From $x = -3$ to $x = 4$: walk 3 units to reach 0, then 4 more units. That is $3 + 4 = 7$, which is $|-3| + |4|$. From 2 to 6 on the same side, you only walk the extra part: $6 - 2 = 4$. Counting the grid squares gives the same answers.

blocks.title: Opposite sides of 0
blocks.q: Find the distance between $(-3, 2)$ and $(4, 2)$.
steps: Same y, so the segment is horizontal. Use the x-coordinates, $-3$ and $4$.
They are on opposite sides of 0: $|-3| + |4| = 3 + 4 = 7$.

blocks.title: Same side of 0
blocks.q: Find the distance between $(2, -1)$ and $(2, -6)$.
steps: Same x, so the segment is vertical. Use $-1$ and $-6$.

blocks.q: On a town map, the school is at $(-5, 1)$ and the library at $(3, 1)$. Each unit is one block. How far apart are they?
steps: Same y: use $-5$ and $3$, on opposite sides of 0.

blocks.html: Subtracting the digits across 0: from $-3$ to 4, "$4 - 3 = 1$". That ignores the 3 units on the negative side. Quick check: count the squares, or ask whether 0 is between the two numbers. If it is, add.

blocks.html: You have written powers of 10 like $10^3 = 10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1,000$. The same short way of writing works for any number.
$b^n$ means $b$ used as a factor $n$ times. The base $b$ is the number multiplied; the exponent $n$ counts the factors: $2^4 = 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 16$.

Multiplication is a short way to write repeated addition: $4 + 4 + 4 = 3 \times 4$. An exponent is a short way to write repeated multiplication: $4 \times 4 \times 4 = 4^3$. That is why the exponent counts how many times the base appears, not something to multiply by. Squares and cubes get their names from shapes: $4^2$ is the number of unit squares in a 4 by 4 square, and $3^3$ is the number of unit cubes in a 3 by 3 by 3 cube.

blocks.cap: A cube 3 units on each edge holds $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 3^3 = 27$ unit cubes. Drag to turn it.

blocks.html: Multiplying the base by the exponent: $2^4$ is not $2 \times 4 = 8$. Quick check: write out the factors. $2^4 = 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2$, which is 16. The table shows the difference grows fast: $2^6 = 64$, but $2 \times 6$ is only 12.

blocks.html: You know the order of operations for parentheses, multiplying, dividing, adding and subtracting. Exponents fit in right after the grouping symbols.
Work in this order: (1) grouping symbols, (2) exponents, (3) multiply and divide from left to right, (4) add and subtract from left to right.

An exponent is a product that has been bundled up: $2^2$ is $2 \times 2$. In $3 \times 2^2$ the exponent belongs only to the 2, so that bundle is finished first: $3 \times (2 \times 2) = 12$. If we wanted $(3 \times 2)^2 = 36$, we would have written the parentheses. Everyone using the same order means an expression has only one value.

blocks.html: In Grade 3 you used a letter for an unknown number in an equation. Letters, called variables, can also stand for a number that changes from one situation to the next.
A variable is a letter that stands for a number. Writing a number next to a letter means multiply: $3a$ means $3 \times a$.

blocks.cap: $3a$ is three equal lengths $a$; $a + 3$ is one length $a$ and 3 more. Different expressions, different amounts.

blocks.html: If pencils cost \$2 each, then 1 pencil costs \$2, 5 pencils cost \$10, and $n$ pencils cost $2n$ dollars. The one expression $2n$ describes every case at once, because $n$ can be any number of pencils. That is the power of a variable: it lets us write a rule instead of a long list.

That is the cost of 4 pens.

blocks.html: Treating a letter as a label: reading $3a$ as "3 apples". In math, $a$ stands for a number, like the number of apples or the price of one apple, and $3a$ is 3 times that number. Quick check: put a number in for the letter and see if the expression still makes sense.

Turn each phrase into an operation, in the order the words describe: "5 more than $n$" is $n + 5$, "5 less than $n$" is $n - 5$, "3 times the sum of $y$ and 4" is $3(y + 4)$.

blocks.html: As you write expressions, it helps to have names for their parts, so we can talk about them clearly.
Terms are the parts that are added (or subtracted). A coefficient is the number multiplying a variable. A constant is a term with no variable. A factor is something that is multiplied.

$2(x + 3) + 4y + 7$

blocks.html: Parentheses group a sum into a single quantity. In $2(x + 3)$, the 2 multiplies the whole sum, so $2(x + 3)$ is one term: a product of the two factors 2 and $(x + 3)$. The + sign inside the parentheses is part of that factor, so it does not split the expression into more terms. A letter written alone, like $y$, has coefficient 1, because $y = 1 \cdot y$.

steps: The terms are $5m$, $n$ and $9$: three terms.
$n$ is $1 \cdot n$, so its coefficient is 1.

blocks.q: How many terms are in $6(a + 2) + 3a$?

The second factor is itself a sum of two terms, $k$ and 1.

blocks.html: Counting the + inside parentheses as a new term, so that $6(a + 2) + 3a$ seems to have 3 terms. Quick check: only + and − signs that are outside every parentheses separate terms. Another slip is saying $n$ has no coefficient; it has coefficient 1.

blocks.html: To evaluate an expression, put in a number for each variable you wrote and work it out with the order of operations.
Substitute: replace each variable with its value, in parentheses if that helps. Then simplify in the usual order. $3x + 5$ when $x = 4$ is $3(4) + 5 = 17$.

A variable stands for a number. Once you know the number, the expression is an ordinary numerical expression, so all the rules you already know apply. Writing the value in parentheses keeps the operations visible: $3x$ with $x = 4$ becomes $3(4)$, which means $3 \times 4$, not the number 34.

blocks.html: You used the distributive property to factor sums of numbers like $36 + 8 = 4(9 + 2)$. It works the same way with variables, and it lets you rewrite an expression without changing its value.
Equivalent expressions are equal for every value of the variable. The distributive property, $a(b + c) = ab + ac$, makes them: $3(x + 2) = 3x + 6$. So does combining like terms: $y + y + y = 3y$.

Since it is the same rectangle, the two expressions are equal whatever length $x$ is. Combining like terms is the same property: $4a + 3a = (4 + 3)a = 7a$.

$4a + 3a = 7a$. The 2 has no $a$, so it stays.

blocks.html: Now that you can make equivalent expressions, how do you decide whether two given expressions are equivalent?

Two expressions are equivalent when one can be rewritten into the other with properties (distributive, commutative, combining like terms). Then they are equal for every value of the variable. One value where they differ proves they are not equivalent.

Properties of numbers are always true, so if properties turn one expression into the other, the two must agree for every number you put in. Testing values works in one direction only. A single mismatch settles it: not equivalent. But a single match proves nothing, because two different expressions can happen to agree at one value.

blocks.html: Deciding by checking a single value. Quick check: to show two expressions are equivalent, rewrite one into the other. To show they are not, find one value where they differ. Picking an unusual value like $x = 2$ or $x = 10$ catches more mistakes than $x = 0$ or $x = 1$.

blocks.html: The equal sign says both sides name the same amount. When an equation has a variable, it is true for some values and false for others. You can evaluate each side to find out which.
A solution is a value of the variable that makes the equation true. To check a value, substitute it and see whether both sides are equal.

blocks.name: balance
blocks.cap: With each bag weighing 4, the scale is level: $2(4) + 1 = 9$, so $x = 4$ is a solution.

blocks.html: Substituting turns the equation into a plain statement about numbers, which is either true or false. $2x + 1 = 9$ with $x = 4$ becomes $2(4) + 1 = 9$, that is $9 = 9$: true. With $x = 3$ it becomes $7 = 9$: false. The equation is a question, "which number makes this true?", and a solution is an answer to it.

blocks.title: Check a value
blocks.q: Is $x = 4$ a solution of $2x + 1 = 9$?

blocks.title: A value that fails
blocks.q: Is $n = 6$ a solution of $\frac{n}{3} = 3$?

blocks.title: An inequality has many solutions
blocks.q: Which of 2, 3, 4 and 5 make $x + 4 > 7$ true?

blocks.html: Two slips: stopping after working out one side, and forgetting what the sign asks for. In $x + 4 > 7$, the value 3 gives $7 > 7$, which is false: "greater than" does not include "equal to". Quick check: write the whole statement with the number in it and read it aloud. Is it true?

blocks.html: You can check a solution by substituting. Now you will find it. Think of the equation as a balance: both sides weigh the same.
To undo adding a number, subtract it from both sides. To undo subtracting a number, add it to both sides. $x + 5 = 12$ becomes $x = 12 - 5 = 7$.

blocks.name: balance
blocks.cap: Take the same thing off both pans to keep the scale level. Try "One side only" to see it tip.

blocks.html: If two amounts are equal and you take 5 away from each, they are still equal. Take 5 from only one side and the scale tips: the sides are no longer equal. Subtracting 5 is the right move because it undoes adding 5: $(x + 5) - 5 = x$, which leaves $x$ alone on its side.

blocks.title: Undo adding
blocks.q: Solve $x + 5 = 12$.

blocks.title: With fractions
blocks.q: Solve $\frac{2}{3} + y = \frac{5}{4}$.

blocks.name: tapediagram
blocks.cap: The same equation as a tape: 12 is made of 5 and the unknown part, $x$.

blocks.html: Subtracting on one side only, or adding when you should subtract. For $x + 5 = 12$, writing $x = 12 + 5 = 17$ undoes nothing. Quick check: substitute your answer. $17 + 5 = 22$, not 12, so it is wrong; $7 + 5 = 12$ is right.

blocks.html: Some equations multiply or divide the variable instead of adding to it. The balance idea from One-Step Equations with Adding and Subtracting still works: do the same thing to both sides.
To undo multiplying by a number, divide both sides by it. To undo dividing by a number, multiply both sides by it. $4x = 12$ becomes $x = 12 \div 4 = 3$.

blocks.name: balance
blocks.cap: Four equal bags balance 12 cubes. Split both sides into 4 equal groups.

blocks.html: $4x = 12$ says four equal bags weigh 12. Split each side into 4 equal groups and keep one group from each: one bag on the left, 3 cubes on the right. Still balanced. Dividing by 4 undoes multiplying by 4, because $4x \div 4 = x$.

blocks.title: Undo multiplying
blocks.q: Solve $4x = 12$.

blocks.title: Undo dividing
blocks.q: Solve $\frac{m}{5} = 7$.

blocks.title: A fraction coefficient
blocks.q: Solve $\frac{2}{3}k = 10$.
steps: Multiply both sides by the reciprocal, $\frac{3}{2}$ (that is the same as dividing by $\frac{2}{3}$).

blocks.html: Subtracting the coefficient: solving $4x = 12$ as $x = 12 - 4 = 8$. The 4 is multiplying $x$, not added to it. Quick check: $4x$ means $4 \times x$, and $4 \times 8 = 32$, not 12.

blocks.html: An equation is a sentence about numbers. If you can say a story as an equation, you can solve it with the one-step moves from One-Step Equations with Multiplying and Dividing and the topics before it. Use expressions for the parts of the story.
(1) Choose a letter for the unknown. (2) Write the story as an equation. (3) Solve it. (4) Check the answer in the story, not just the equation.

blocks.name: tapediagram
blocks.cap: Money spent (18) and money left (27) together make the money at the start.

blocks.html: The equation says the same thing as the story, only in symbols, so any number that makes the equation true also makes the story true. Checking in the story catches the case where the equation was written the wrong way round.

blocks.title: Money left
blocks.q: After spending \$18, Kai has \$27 left. How much did Kai have at first?
steps: Let $m$ be the money at first. Spending 18 leaves 27: $m - 18 = 27$.
Check in the story: \$45 − \$18 = \$27 left. Yes.

blocks.title: Equal rows
blocks.q: 84 chairs are set out in 6 equal rows. How many chairs are in each row?
steps: Let $r$ be the chairs in a row. 6 rows of $r$ make 84: $6r = 84$.

blocks.title: Equal pieces
blocks.q: A rope is cut into 5 equal pieces, each 1.2 meters long. How long was the rope?
steps: Let $L$ be the rope’s length. Cutting it into 5 equal pieces: $\frac{L}{5} = 1.2$.

blocks.html: Choosing the operation from one key word. "Left" in the first story leads to subtraction in the equation, $m - 18 = 27$, but solving it takes addition. If you subtract to get the answer, $27 - 18 = 9$, you get a starting amount smaller than what is left. Quick check: put your answer back into the story and read it.

blocks.html: An equation like $x = 3$ has one solution. An inequality like $x > 3$ has infinitely many: 3.1, 4, 7.5, 100, … You can order numbers, so you can picture all of them at once on a number line.

$x > 3$ means every number greater than 3. To graph it, draw an open circle at 3 (3 is not included) and shade to the right. For $\ge$ or $\le$, the circle is closed (filled), because the boundary is included.

blocks.name: g6-ineq
blocks.cap: Pick a sign, move the boundary, and slide the test number to see which numbers are solutions.

blocks.html: There are too many solutions to list, so we draw them: the shaded ray holds every solution. The circle answers one small question: is the boundary itself a solution? For $x > 3$, try 3: $3 > 3$ is false, so the circle is left open. For $x \ge 3$, $3 \ge 3$ is true, so the circle is filled in.

blocks.q: Graph $x \le -1$.
steps: $\le$ includes $-1$, so draw a closed circle at $-1$.
Less than means to the left: shade left from $-1$.
blocks.a: A closed circle at $-1$ with the ray shaded to the left.

blocks.q: Riders must be at least 48 inches tall. Write an inequality for a rider’s height $h$.

blocks.title: Read it from the variable
blocks.q: What does $3 < x$ mean?
steps: Read it right to left, starting with $x$: $x$ is greater than 3.
So $3 < x$ is the same as $x > 3$. The pointed end of the sign always faces the smaller side.

blocks.html: Using a closed circle for $>$, or reading $3 < x$ as "$x$ is less than 3". Quick check: test a number. Is 3 a solution of $x > 3$? $3 > 3$ is false, so the circle must be open. Is 5 a solution of $3 < x$? $3 < 5$ is true, so the shading goes toward 5, to the right.

blocks.html: Many quantities change together: the more hours you work, the more you earn. You have seen pairs like these in ratio graphs, and you can now write equations for them.

The independent variable is the one that changes on its own or that we choose. The dependent variable changes because of it. An equation like $d = 50t$ gives the dependent variable ($d$) from the independent one ($t$). On a graph, the independent variable goes on the horizontal axis.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: A car at 50 miles per hour: time $t$ (hours) across, distance $d$ (miles) up. Drag the point along the line.

blocks.html: A table, a graph and an equation are three views of the same pairs. The table lists some pairs, the graph shows all of them as a line, and the equation is the rule that makes every pair. Putting the independent variable across the bottom lets you read the graph like a story: as time goes on (to the right), distance goes up.

head: $t$ (hours)
blocks.cap: Each hour adds 50 miles: $d = 50t$.

blocks.title: Which is which?
blocks.q: A plant grows 3 cm each week. Let $w$ be the number of weeks and $g$ the growth in cm. Which variable is dependent? Write an equation.
steps: The growth depends on how many weeks have passed, so $g$ is dependent and $w$ is independent.

blocks.title: A starting amount
blocks.q: A pool already has 50 gallons and fills at 20 gallons per minute. Write an equation for the gallons $G$ after $m$ minutes, and find $G$ when $m = 6$.
steps: Start with 50 and add 20 for each minute: $G = 20m + 50$.

blocks.html: Putting the dependent variable on the horizontal axis. Quick check: ask "which one changes because of the other?" That one is dependent and goes up the side. Time is almost always independent.

blocks.html: You know the area of a rectangle is length times width, even with fraction side lengths. A parallelogram leans over, but you can turn it into a rectangle without changing its area.

The area of a parallelogram is base times height: $A = bh$. The height is the distance straight across from the base to the opposite side, measured at a right angle to the base, not along the slanted side.

blocks.name: areaformulas
blocks.cap: Press Rearrange: the triangle cut from one end slides to the other end, and the parallelogram becomes a 6 by 4 rectangle.

blocks.html: Cut along the height to take a right triangle off one end, and slide it to the other end. The pieces now form a rectangle. Nothing was added or lost, so the area is the same. The rectangle's length is the parallelogram's base, and its width is the parallelogram's height, so the area is $b \times h$.

blocks.title: Base and height
blocks.q: A parallelogram has base 9 cm and height 5 cm. Find its area.

blocks.title: Ignore the slanted side
blocks.q: A parallelogram has a base of 7.5 cm, slanted sides of 5 cm, and a height of 4 cm. Find its area.
steps: The height is 4 cm; the 5 cm side leans, so it is not the height.

blocks.name: g6-shape
blocks.cap: The dashed height meets the base at a right angle. The slanted side is longer than the height.

blocks.title: Work backward
blocks.q: A parallelogram has an area of 54 square inches and a base of 9 inches. What is its height?

blocks.html: Multiplying the base by the slanted side. In the second example that gives $7.5 \times 5 = 37.5$, which is too big. Quick check: push a parallelogram over until it is almost flat. Its sides keep their lengths, but its area shrinks toward 0, so the slanted side cannot be what decides the area. Only the height can.

blocks.html: A triangle is half of a parallelogram, and that tells you its area.
The area of a triangle is half of base times height: $A = \frac{1}{2}bh$. The height is measured at a right angle to the base, from the opposite corner.

blocks.name: areaformulas
blocks.cap: Press Rearrange: a copy of the triangle, turned halfway around, completes a parallelogram.

blocks.html: Take two copies of any triangle and turn one of them halfway around. They fit together into a parallelogram with the same base and the same height. The parallelogram's area is $bh$, and the triangle is exactly half of it, so its area is $\frac{1}{2}bh$.

blocks.title: Base and height
blocks.q: A triangle has base 10 m and height 6 m. Find its area.

blocks.title: A right triangle
blocks.q: A right triangle has sides 6, 8 and 10 inches. Find its area.
steps: The two sides that meet at the right angle, 6 and 8, are a base and its height.
$A = \frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 8 = 24$. The 10-inch side is slanted and not needed.

blocks.title: The height outside the triangle
blocks.q: A triangle has a base of 5 cm. The height from the top corner, 4 cm, falls outside the triangle, on the extended base. Find the area.
steps: The height still meets the line of the base at a right angle; it just lands beyond the base.

blocks.name: g6-shape
blocks.cap: In a triangle with a wide angle, the height can fall outside. The base line is extended with a dashed line to meet it.

blocks.html: Forgetting the $\frac{1}{2}$, or using a slanted side as the height. Quick check: the triangle fits inside a rectangle that is $b$ wide and $h$ tall, so its area must be less than $b \times h$. If your answer equals $b \times h$, you forgot the half.

sources.name: OpenStax, Prealgebra 2e, section 9.4 Use Properties of Rectangles, Triangles, and Trapezoids
Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 6.G.A.1: area of triangles

blocks.html: A trapezoid has one pair of parallel sides, called its bases. The same trick that worked for the triangle, two copies make a parallelogram, works here too.
The area of a trapezoid is $A = \frac{1}{2}(b_1 + b_2)h$: add the two parallel sides, multiply by the height, and take half.

blocks.name: areaformulas
blocks.cap: Press Rearrange: a turned copy of the trapezoid completes a parallelogram whose base is $7 + 3$.

blocks.html: Put a copy of the trapezoid next to it, turned upside down. The long base of one lines up with the short base of the other, so together they make a parallelogram with base $b_1 + b_2$ and the same height. Its area is $(b_1 + b_2)h$, and the trapezoid is half of it.

blocks.title: Use the formula
blocks.q: A trapezoid has bases 10 ft and 6 ft and height 4 ft. Find its area.

blocks.title: With decimals
blocks.q: Find the area of a trapezoid with bases 7.5 m and 4.5 m and height 3 m.

blocks.title: Another way: split it
blocks.q: A trapezoid has bases 9 and 5 and height 4, with its slanted side on the right. Split it into a rectangle and a triangle.

blocks.html: Using a slanted side instead of the height, or adding all four sides. Only the two parallel sides go in the formula, and the height must be straight across between them. Quick check: the area must be between $b_2 \times h$ and $b_1 \times h$ (for the first example, between $6 \times 4 = 24$ and $10 \times 4 = 40$).

blocks.html: Most shapes are not a rectangle, triangle or trapezoid. But almost any polygon can be cut into those shapes, or seen as one of them with a piece missing.
To find the area of a composite polygon, split it into rectangles and triangles and add their areas, or start with a bigger shape and subtract the part that is missing.

blocks.name: g6-shape
blocks.cap: An L-shaped floor, split by the dashed line into two rectangles.

blocks.html: Area counts unit squares. Cutting a shape into pieces does not create or remove any squares, so the pieces' areas add up to the whole. Taking a piece away removes exactly that piece's squares, which is why subtracting works too.

blocks.title: Add the pieces
blocks.q: Find the area of the L-shaped floor in the picture.
steps: Left rectangle: 6 m by 8 m, so $6 \times 8 = 48$.
Right rectangle: $11 - 6 = 5$ m by 3 m, so $5 \times 3 = 15$.

blocks.title: Subtract the missing piece
blocks.q: Find the same area by subtracting.
steps: The full rectangle would be 11 by 8: 88.

blocks.title: A rectangle and a triangle
blocks.q: A house shape is a 6 by 5 rectangle with a triangle on top, base 6 and height 3. Find its area.

blocks.name: geoboard
blocks.cap: Drag the corners. Split the shape in your head and check your total against the area shown.

blocks.html: Two things go wrong: using a side length that is not given directly (it often has to be found, like $11 - 6 = 5$), and counting an overlap twice. Quick check: work it out two ways, adding and subtracting. Both should give the same area.

Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, 6.G.A.1: area of polygons by decomposing

blocks.html: Put a polygon on the coordinate plane and its side lengths come from the coordinates. Use distances on the grid for sides, and area ideas for the inside.
Plot the vertices and join them in order. A side along a grid line has length equal to the distance between the coordinates that change. Use those lengths for perimeter and area.

blocks.name: geoboard
blocks.cap: Rectangle ABCD across four quadrants. Drag a corner and watch the lengths and area.

blocks.html: Moving from A to B changes only x, from $-3$ to 4, so AB is horizontal and its length is the distance between $-3$ and 4. That is the same as walking along the x-axis: 3 units to 0, then 4 more. The coordinates turn geometry into number lines you already know.

blocks.title: Perimeter and area
blocks.q: Rectangle ABCD has vertices $A(-3, -2)$, $B(4, -2)$, $C(4, 3)$ and $D(-3, 3)$. Find its perimeter and area.

blocks.title: The missing vertex
blocks.q: Three vertices of a rectangle are $(-2, 1)$, $(5, 1)$ and $(5, -4)$. Find the fourth.
steps: Each x-coordinate and each y-coordinate of a rectangle like this is used twice.
x: $-2$ is used once. y: $-4$ is used once.

blocks.title: A right triangle
blocks.q: Find the area of the triangle with vertices $(-2, 1)$, $(3, 1)$ and $(-2, 5)$.
steps: The horizontal side has length $2 + 3 = 5$ and the vertical side has length $5 - 1 = 4$.
They meet at a right angle at $(-2, 1)$: $A = \frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 4 = 10$.

blocks.html: Subtracting coordinates on opposite sides of 0 as if they were on the same side: the side from $x = -3$ to $x = 4$ is 7, not 1. Quick check: count the grid squares along one side.

blocks.html: A box is made of flat faces. Unfold it and you get a flat pattern called a net. Each face is a rectangle or a triangle whose area you can find.
The surface area of a solid is the total area of all its faces, which is the area of its net. For a box: $SA = 2\ell w + 2\ell h + 2wh$.

blocks.name: nets
blocks.cap: The net of a 4 by 3 by 2 box. Fold it up and unfold it: the six faces are the same pieces either way.

blocks.html: Folding and unfolding moves faces around but does not stretch or shrink any of them, so the total area stays the same. Laying the faces flat lets you see every one, including the bottom and the back, which are hidden when the box sits on a table. Opposite faces of a box match, which is why each area appears twice in the formula.

blocks.title: A box
blocks.q: Find the surface area of a box 4 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm tall.

blocks.title: A cube
blocks.q: Find the surface area of a cube with 5-inch edges.
steps: A cube has 6 square faces, each $5 \times 5 = 25$.

blocks.title: A square pyramid
blocks.q: A pyramid has a square base 6 m on a side, and each triangular face has height 5 m. Find its surface area.

blocks.html: Missing the hidden faces (like the bottom of a box) or counting a face twice. Quick check: count the faces before adding. A box has 6, a square pyramid has 5 (1 square and 4 triangles), and a triangular prism has 5 (2 triangles and 3 rectangles).

blocks.html: You found the volume of a box by counting layers of unit cubes: $V = \ell wh$. When the edges are fractions, the cubes do not fit exactly, but smaller cubes do.

$V = \ell \times w \times h$ works for fraction edge lengths too: a box $2\frac{1}{2}$ by 1 by $1\frac{1}{2}$ has volume $\frac{5}{2} \times 1 \times \frac{3}{2} = \frac{15}{4} = 3\frac{3}{4}$ cubic units.

blocks.name: volume
blocks.cap: A box built from cubes with $\frac{1}{2}$-unit edges: 5 by 2 by 3 small cubes. Drag to turn it.

blocks.html: Fill the box with cubes whose edges are $\frac{1}{2}$ unit. Eight of them make one unit cube (2 by 2 by 2), so each is $\frac{1}{8}$ of a cubic unit. Along the edges fit $5$, $2$ and $3$ small cubes, so $5 \times 2 \times 3 = 30$ small cubes fill the box: $30 \times \frac{1}{8} = \frac{30}{8} = 3\frac{3}{4}$. Multiplying the edges, using fraction multiplication, gives the same number.

blocks.title: Multiply the edges
blocks.q: Find the volume of a box $2\frac{1}{2}$ ft by 1 ft by $1\frac{1}{2}$ ft.

blocks.title: Count small cubes
blocks.q: How many cubes with $\frac{1}{2}$-inch edges fill a box 3 in by 2 in by $1\frac{1}{2}$ in?

blocks.title: A cube
blocks.q: Find the volume of a cube with edges $\frac{3}{2}$ m.

blocks.html: Multiplying mixed numbers piece by piece: $2\frac{1}{2} \times 1\frac{1}{2}$ is not $2 \times 1$ plus $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}$. Quick check: change mixed numbers to fractions first, and estimate. $2\frac{1}{2} \times 1\frac{1}{2}$ is between $2 \times 1 = 2$ and $3 \times 2 = 6$; the true value is $3\frac{3}{4}$.

blocks.html: You have made line plots of measurements. Statistics starts one step earlier, with the question you ask.

A statistical question expects answers that vary, so you collect many pieces of data to answer it. "How many hours do the students in my class sleep?" is statistical. "How many hours did I sleep last night?" is not.

blocks.name: dotplot
blocks.cap: Answers to "How many hours did the students in our class sleep last night?" They vary, so we describe the whole set.

blocks.html: If every answer would be the same, one look settles the question; there is nothing to summarize. Statistics is about data that vary: it asks what is typical, how spread out the answers are, and what shape they make. A question that expects variety is what makes those ideas useful.

head: Question
Statistical?
Why
rows: How old are the people at the library today?
How tall is our school’s flagpole?
How tall are the sunflowers in the garden?
heights vary from plant to plant
blocks.cap: Statistical questions ask about a group with varied answers.

blocks.title: Is it statistical?
blocks.q: Is "How many pets do the families on our street have?" a statistical question?
steps: It asks every family, and different families have different numbers of pets.

blocks.title: Make it statistical
blocks.q: Change "How far is my walk to school?" into a statistical question.
steps: The question has one answer because it is about one person.
Ask about a group instead, where the answers will differ.
blocks.a: For example: "How far do the students in my class walk to school?"

blocks.html: Calling a question statistical because it has a number in its answer. "How old am I?" is answered with a number, but only one number. Quick check: imagine collecting the answers. Would you get a list of different values? If not, it is not statistical.

blocks.html: Data from a statistical question is easier to understand in a picture. Two common pictures are the dot plot and the histogram.

A dot plot puts one dot above a number line for each value. A histogram groups the values into equal intervals and draws a bar for each interval; the bar's height is how many values fall in it, and the bars touch.

blocks.name: dotplot
blocks.cap: A dot plot of how many pets 13 students have. Each dot is one student.

blocks.name: g6-histogram
blocks.cap: A histogram of 22 travel times. Change the interval width and watch the shape get finer or coarser.

blocks.html: A dot plot keeps every single value, which is perfect for a small set of whole numbers. With many values spread over a wide range, a dot plot gets crowded, so a histogram counts how many values land in each interval instead. The intervals must be the same width so that taller really means "more values", and they meet with no gaps so every value has exactly one place to go. That is why the bars touch.

blocks.title: Read a dot plot
blocks.q: In the dot plot of pets, how many students have more than 2 pets?
steps: Count the dots to the right of 2: above 3, 4 and 6.

blocks.title: Build a histogram
blocks.q: Sort these travel times into intervals 0–9, 10–19, 20–29 and 30–39: 5, 12, 25, 8, 31, 14, 19, 22, 3, 15.

blocks.html: Leaving gaps between histogram bars, or using intervals of different widths. A gap suggests some values are missing; a wide interval collects more values just because it is wide, so its bar looks important when it is not. Quick check: every interval should hold the same span of numbers, and each interval should start where the last one ended.

blocks.html: Looking at a dot plot, we often want one number that says what is typical. The mean is one such number, and you already know how to compute it with division.
The mean is the sum of the values divided by how many values there are. It is the fair share: the amount each would get if the total were shared out evenly.

Picture four stacks of cubes, 3, 7, 5 and 9 tall. Move cubes from the tall stacks to the short ones until every stack is the same height. No cubes are added or lost, so the total is still $3 + 7 + 5 + 9 = 24$, now in 4 equal stacks: $24 \div 4 = 6$ each. That leveled height is the mean. The mean is also the balance point of a dot plot: the values above it and below it pull equally.

blocks.name: dotplot
blocks.cap: The red triangle marks the mean, the balance point. Drag dots to make the mean 6.

blocks.title: Find the mean
blocks.q: Find the mean of 3, 7, 5 and 9.

blocks.title: Test scores
blocks.q: Find the mean of the scores 85, 90, 78, 92 and 80.

blocks.title: A missing value
blocks.q: The mean of four numbers is 7. Three of them are 5, 9 and 6. What is the fourth?
steps: Mean 7 for 4 numbers means the total is $4 \times 7 = 28$.
The three known numbers add to 20.

blocks.html: Dividing by the wrong count, especially when some values are 0. The data 0, 4, 5 has three values, so the mean is $9 \div 3 = 3$, not $9 \div 2$. Quick check: the mean must lie between the smallest and the largest value.

blocks.html: The mean is one way to describe the center of data. The median and the mode are two others, and you find them by looking at a dot plot or an ordered list.
The median is the middle value when the data are in order. With an even number of values, it is the mean of the two middle values. The mode is the value that appears most often.

blocks.name: dotplot
blocks.cap: Nine values: the median is the 5th from the left. The mode is the tallest stack. Drag a dot and watch them.

blocks.html: The median splits the data into two halves with the same number of values on each side. Only the order matters, not how far away the values are, so one very large or very small value hardly moves it. That is what makes the median a sturdy description of "the middle".

blocks.title: Odd number of values
blocks.q: Find the median of 7, 2, 9, 4 and 5.
steps: Five values, so the middle one is the 3rd: 5.

blocks.title: Even number of values
blocks.q: Find the median of 3, 8, 6, 10, 1 and 12.
steps: Six values: the middle two are 6 and 8.

blocks.title: The mode
blocks.q: Find the mode of 4, 7, 4, 9, 7, 4, 2.
steps: Count each value: 4 appears 3 times, 7 twice, 9 and 2 once.

blocks.html: Taking the middle of the list as it is given, without putting it in order. For 7, 2, 9, 4, 5 the middle of the unordered list is 9, which is the largest value, not the middle one. Quick check: the median should have as many values below it as above it.

blocks.html: Center is only half the story. Two classes can have the same median score but very different spreads. Range and interquartile range measure spread.

Range = greatest value − least value. The interquartile range (IQR) = $Q_3 - Q_1$, the spread of the middle half of the data. $Q_1$ is the median of the lower half and $Q_3$ is the median of the upper half.

blocks.name: boxplot
blocks.cap: The box covers the middle half of the data, from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$. Its width is the IQR. Drag a dot to see what changes.

blocks.html: The range uses only the two most extreme values, so one unusual value can stretch it a lot. The IQR leaves out the lowest quarter and the highest quarter of the data, so it describes where the middle half lives, and an outlier hardly changes it.

blocks.title: An even number of values
blocks.q: Find the range and IQR of 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15.

blocks.title: An odd number of values
blocks.q: Find the IQR of 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 20.
steps: The median is 8, the middle value. Leave it out of both halves.
IQR $= 11 - 5 = 6$. (The range is $20 - 3 = 17$, stretched by the 20.)

blocks.html: Forgetting to order the data first, or putting the median into one of the halves when there is an odd number of values. Math Ladder leaves the middle value out of both halves, as many U.S. courses do. Quick check: the two halves should have the same number of values.

blocks.html: The median and the quartiles you found for the IQR split data into four parts. A box plot draws them.

A box plot shows the five-number summary: minimum, $Q_1$, median, $Q_3$, maximum. The box runs from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$ with a line at the median, and whiskers reach out to the minimum and maximum. Each of the four sections holds about a quarter of the data.

blocks.name: boxplot
blocks.cap: Each shaded part holds about 25% of the values, whether it is long or short.

blocks.html: The five numbers cut the ordered data into four groups with about the same number of values. A box plot places those cuts on a number line, so you can see the center (the median line) and the spread (the width of the box and the whiskers) at a glance. A long section means its values are spread over a wide range, not that it holds more of them.

blocks.title: Make the summary
blocks.q: Find the five-number summary of 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 15, 16, 21.
steps: Minimum 4, maximum 21. Nine values, so the median is the 5th: 10.

blocks.title: Read a box plot
blocks.q: In a box plot, $Q_3 = 30$. About what percent of the data is above 30?
steps: Above $Q_3$ is the right whisker: one of the four sections.

blocks.html: Thinking a longer section of a box plot holds more data points. In the plot above, the right whisker (15.5 to 21) is longer than the left one (4 to 6.5), but each holds about a quarter of the values. Quick check: count the dots in each section, not the length.

blocks.html: The IQR measures spread around the median. To measure spread around the mean, we use distances, which are absolute values.
The mean absolute deviation (MAD) is the average distance of the values from the mean. Find the mean, find each value's distance from it, then find the mean of those distances.

blocks.name: dotplot
blocks.cap: Each orange line is one value’s distance from the mean. The MAD is the average length of the lines.

blocks.html: If you subtract the mean from each value and keep the signs, the results always add to 0: the mean is the balance point, so what is above it exactly cancels what is below it. Averaging those signed differences would say every data set has no spread. Distances are never negative, so they cannot cancel, and their average measures how far a typical value is from the mean.

blocks.title: Find the MAD
blocks.q: Find the MAD of 10, 12, 15, 18, 20.

blocks.cap: The signed differences cancel to 0; the distances add to 16.

blocks.title: Compare spreads
blocks.q: Set A: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Set B: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Both have mean 6. Which has the greater MAD?
blocks.a: Set B: its values are farther from the mean.

blocks.html: Averaging the signed differences, which always gives 0. Quick check: the MAD can only be 0 when every value equals the mean. If your data vary and you got 0, take the absolute values.

blocks.html: Now you can measure center (mean, median) and spread (IQR, MAD), and you can draw box plots. To describe a data set well, say three things: its center, its spread and its shape.

For data that are roughly symmetric, the mean and MAD describe it well. For data that are skewed or have outliers, use the median and IQR, because extreme values pull the mean and MAD but barely move the median and IQR.

blocks.name: dotplot
blocks.cap: Drag the 30 all the way to the right end. The mean slides toward it; the median stays put.

blocks.html: The mean uses the size of every value, so one value far away drags it toward itself. The median only uses the order, so moving the largest value farther away does not change which value is in the middle. Spread works the same way: the MAD averages distances, which an outlier makes bigger, while the IQR ignores the top and bottom quarters.

blocks.title: An outlier
blocks.q: Phone-call times in minutes: 22, 24, 25, 25, 26, 28, 95. Which describes a typical call better, the mean or the median?
steps: Six of the seven calls are 28 minutes or less, so 35 is not typical. The 95 pulled the mean up.

blocks.title: Describe the shape
blocks.q: Most students read 1 to 3 books, a few read 6, 8 or 10. Describe the shape.
steps: The values pile up on the left and trail off in a long tail to the right.
blocks.a: Skewed right; describe it with the median and IQR.

blocks.cap: Two teams with similar centers but very different spreads.

blocks.html: Reporting the mean for skewed data with an outlier. Quick check: compare the mean and median. If they are far apart, the data are skewed or have an outlier, and the median is the better description of a typical value.
